draft.title: Why adjustments are made
card: A business reports its profit for a set period, such as a year. Revenue and expenses must be matched to the period they relate to.
Cash does not always move in the same period as the revenue or expense. A bill may be paid early, or paid late, or money may arrive after the work is done.
At the end of the period, called balance day, the business makes adjusting entries. These move revenue and expenses into the period they belong to.
Without adjustments, profit would be overstated or understated, and assets and liabilities would be wrong in the reports.
draft.remember: Adjustments match revenue and expenses to the period they relate to, not to when cash moves.

a.q: Why does a business make adjustments on balance day?
opts: To place revenue and expenses in the period they relate to
To record every cash payment on the day it is made
To make sure profit is as high as possible each year
To remove all assets and liabilities from the records
a.why: Adjustments fix the timing of revenue and expenses so profit for the period is reported fairly. They are not about raising profit: the aim is a fair figure, which may be higher or lower.
a.clue: Think about which period the revenue or expense belongs to.

b.q: Jas runs a gym in Bendigo. On balance day, 30 June, she has used electricity for June but the bill arrives in July. If she makes no adjustment, what is the effect on the June report?
opts: Expenses are understated and profit is overstated
Expenses are overstated and profit is understated
Revenue is understated and profit is overstated
Expenses and profit are both unaffected
b.why: June's electricity was used in June, so it is a June expense even though no bill has been paid. Leaving it out makes expenses too low and profit too high. Profit is not unaffected just because no cash moved.

a.best: To place revenue and expenses in the period they relate to

b.best: Expenses are understated and profit is overstated
